transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-08
Start time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees: Alex Murray (Redwood AE); Priya Singh (Redwood SE); Jordan Lee (BrightScale - Infra); Maya Patel (BrightScale - ML); Samir Khan (BrightScale - SRE)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focused on throughput tuning: continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs and token limits, KV cache behaviors, and quantization tradeoffs. Customer wants baseline for a dedicated pilot in their VPC/on-prem evaluation. Action items and next steps captured at end.

Topics:
- Continuous batching and prefetching
- Scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, fairness, backpressure)
- Token limits and max_tokens per request impact
- KV cache shard sizing and warmup
- Quantization impacts on latency vs quality (int8/GPTQ/q4_0 family)
- VPC/on-prem constraints and benchmark suggestions

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Murray: Hey everyone thanks for hopping on, uh, we're gonna focus on throughput tuning today. Priya and I will lead, hi BrightScale team.
[00:12] Jordan Lee: Hey thanks Alex, yeah we have Maya and Samir here; our main goal is to see how to push more qps for our summarization pipeline without blowing up latency. We're evaluating dedicated pools in VPC and possibly on-prem.
[00:25] Priya Singh: Cool, can you give a quick baseline numbers? like current latency/p99 and tokens per request?
[00:31] Maya Patel: Right now in our test env we're seeing p99 ~ 420ms for a 256 token summary on A100-ish nodes, avg tokens ~ 230, and peak concurrency ~ 120 concurrent requests. But that's with our DIY batching; we're interested in continuous batching and Redwood's scheduler to improve unit cost.
[00:48] Priya Singh: Got it. So first, continuous batching in Redwood is where we keep an open batch for a short window and add in sequences as they arrive, right? That lets throughput scale with arrival rate without waiting to fill full batch.
[00:58] Alex Murray: Exactly. And the key knobs you'll want to tune are: max_batch_latency (ms), max_num_seqs, and the scheduler's preemptive thresholds. Also token limits per sequence influence memory usage and the decision to shard KV cache.
[01:14] Samir Khan: When we talked to sales we heard "max_num_seqs" — what unit is that and where's the sweet spot?
[01:20] Priya Singh: max_num_seqs is sequences per batch, not tokens. If your sequences are short (like 50-300 tokens), you can push max_num_seqs higher. The sweet spot depends on your model's memory footprint and the GPU. For A100 80GB you might go 32-64 seqs for 8k context models; for H100 you can often go higher. But be careful with kv cache size: large batches plus long contexts can exceed GPU memory.
[01:46] Jordan Lee: We're also doing a 16k context model in some tests. How does that affect continuous batching?
[01:51] Priya Singh: Longer context increases per-seq kv cache, so your effective batch size in tokens explodes. We recommend lowering max_num_seqs and enabling partial KV sharding — Redwood can split KV cache across devices or use disk-backed shards for on-prem if needed. There's also prefetch_kv flag to warm the cache.
[02:08] Alex Murray: Also note our scheduler has a fair-scheduler mode and a high-throughput mode — the fair scheduler cares about latency SLOs and will create smaller batches to protect p99, whereas high-throughput will aggregate more aggressively.
[02:20] Maya Patel: Is that an on/off toggle or configurable?
[02:23] Priya Singh: It's a profile with knobs: target_p99_ms, backpressure_threshold, and max_batch_latency. You can pick a profile and then override the numeric knobs. For example target_p99_ms=350ms, max_batch_latency=20ms, max_num_seqs=40 was our baseline for a 256-token workload in earlier benchmarks.
[02:39] Samir Khan: How does token limit per request affect queueing? We have bursty traffic and some requests are 2k tokens.
[02:45] Priya Singh: Big requests are killers for batching. If one request is 2k tokens, it may consume most of the KV cache for the batch and reduce throughput. Strategies: enforce a max_tokens cap at the API gateway, split long requests into chunked calls, or route large requests to a separate pool with larger instances.
[03:00] Alex Murray: For BrightScale I'd recommend two pools: a latency-sensitive pool with fair-scheduler and smaller max_num_seqs for typical 200-400 token requests, and a large-context pool for >1k tokens with bigger GPUs and different quantization profiles.
[03:13] Jordan Lee: Ok makes sense. On the quantization front, we've seen mixed results — lower precision helps throughput but sometimes quality drops for summarization. What's Redwood's experience?
[03:23] Priya Singh: We provide recommendations by workload. For many summarization tasks q4_0 or GPTQ-4bit variants give 1.5-2x throughput wins with minimal quality regression, but int8 can be viable if you retrain or run evals. We always suggest running perf+quality A/B on a holdout prompt set.
[03:40] Maya Patel: Do quantized models affect KV cache layout or latency differently?
[03:45] Priya Singh: Slightly. Quantized kernels are faster per token but memory layout changes; you may fit larger batches. However some quantized runtimes add a small dequantization step which can add a few ms per token — overall still a net win for throughput. If you have strict p99 SLOs, test end-to-end.
[04:00] Samir Khan: Any guidance on scheduler backpressure? We saw a weird behavior where the queue grew and then latency spiked.
[04:06] Priya Singh: That's classic backpressure misconfig. Increase backpressure_threshold so the scheduler starts rejecting or diverting requests at a lower queue depth, or enable adaptive shedding — Redwood can route overflow traffic to a cheaper pool or a fallback model. Also set max_batch_latency to a low enough value so batches aren't waiting too long for more seqs.
[04:26] Alex Murray: One operational trick: enable per-route token accounting in the console so you can see tokens/sec and sequences/sec per model. That helps tune max_num_seqs and target_p99.
[04:37] Jordan Lee: For our VPC/on-prem tests, network egress is a concern and we need KMS integration with our HSM. Any blockers?
[04:45] Priya Singh: We support customer-managed KMS via standard integrations and HSM through a partner flow. For VPC deployments we can run the runtime in your VPC; on-prem deployments need a small runtime agent and our private control plane options. There are additional audit logs and SOC2 controls available for enterprise.
[04:59] Maya Patel: How should we run benchmarks to capture realistic throughput? We want to emulate our production mix with short and long requests.
[05:06] Priya Singh: Use a mixed workload script. Redwood provides a benchmarker that can replay traffic distributions, with knobs for arrival process (poisson vs bursty), request token distribution, and concurrency. Key metrics: tokens/sec, sequences/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, and GPU memory headroom. Run experiments with quantized and fp16 versions.
[05:24] Alex Murray: We'll share our bench script; Priya will provide a tuned config for your baseline model. Then you'll run it in your VPC/on-prem env and share logs. SE will help interpret.
[05:32] Jordan Lee: Cool. A couple of nitty-gritty Qs: how does continuous batching interact with function calling / tool-calls? We need structured output with small chain-of-thoughts and some function calls that end up with variable token lengths.
[05:45] Priya Singh: Function calling introduces variable-length responses so it's a mix; scheduler treats prompt+response tokens as the sequence length for memory planning. If you have many short tool calls, continuous batching still helps; but if you have occasional huge responses, route those to the large-context pool. There's also a flag to disable batching for certain routes if determinism is required.
[06:06] Samir Khan: You mentioned KV cache warmup earlier, what's best practice?
[06:10] Priya Singh: Warm the cache by replaying common prefixes or recent contexts; Redwood supports a prefetch_kv pipeline that can ingest recent sessions. Also set kv_cache_ttl appropriately: long TTL helps reuse but may increase memory footprint. In our tests, a short 5-15 minute TTL with active prefetch hits 60-80% reuse on chat-like workloads.
[06:26] Maya Patel: For our use-case (multi-tenant summarization) should we shard KV per tenant or global with tenant ids?
[06:32] Priya Singh: Per-tenant sharding helps isolation and eviction fairness but increases overhead. Global KV with tenant tagging is efficient, but eviction policies must avoid noisy neighbors. For BrightScale with ~100 tenants, hybrid approach: group low-traffic tenants into shared shards and give high-volume tenants dedicated shards.
[06:50] Jordan Lee: Any recommendations for scheduler knobs to mitigate noisy neighbor effects?
[06:53] Priya Singh: Yes: per-tenant max_inflight, per-tenant priority weight, and soft quotas. Also configure the scheduler to drop or deprioritize requests from tenants exceeding token quotas.
[07:05] Alex Murray: Quick interjection — on hardware: if you can run H100 or A100 80GB you'll have more headroom for larger max_num_seqs; T4s are fine for smaller models but watch p99.
[07:15] Maya Patel: We're leaning toward a pilot on H100s in our cloud VPC. Cost is a concern — how big is the throughput delta if we move from A100->H100?
[07:24] Priya Singh: For fp16 workloads H100 tends to give 1.2-1.6x throughput depending on kernels and model. For quantized int8/GPTQ the delta can be model-dependent; sometimes H100 benefits less because quantized kernels are already fast. We'll provide benchmark numbers.
[07:38] Samir Khan: On the topic of max tokens, is there a hard upper limit we should enforce at API gateway?
[07:42] Priya Singh: We recommend an enforced soft limit in the gateway for typical routes (e.g. 2k or 4k) and route exceptions to special pools. It prevents big tail requests from degrading overall throughput.
[07:52] Jordan Lee: Okay, let's talk config examples. Can you walk us through a sample config for our latency pool?
[07:58] Priya Singh: Sure. Example: profile: latency-sensitive; target_p99_ms: 350; max_batch_latency_ms: 20; max_num_seqs: 32; backpressure_threshold: 25000 (tokens queued); preempt_mode: true; kv_cache_ttl_min: 10; quantization_profile: q4_0 recommended. For large-context pool: target_p99_ms: 800; max_batch_latency_ms: 50; max_num_seqs: 8; kv_shard_count: 4; quantization_profile: mixed int8/gptq.
[08:25] Alex Murray: We'll put those exact examples in the playbook we share.
[08:29] Maya Patel: When you say backpressure_threshold: 25000 tokens queued, is that global for the node or per-model?
[08:35] Priya Singh: It's configurable by scope. For BrightScale I'd recommend per-route threshold so noisy routes don't impact others. You can also set a global safety threshold.
[08:45] Jordan Lee: If we run the benchmark and see GPU OOMs, what's the typical mitigation path?
[08:50] Priya Singh: First reduce max_num_seqs, lower max_batch_latency (to reduce accumulation), or enable KV sharding across GPUs. If it's persistent, increase instance size or use quantization to reduce memory.
[09:02] Samir Khan: Any tradeoffs to sharding KV across devices?
[09:06] Priya Singh: Sharding spreads memory but adds cross-device communication which can add latency for each token. For high throughput you can overlap comms with compute; Redwood's runtime tries to pipeline those ops, but it depends on model and hardware topology.
[09:19] Alex Murray: A note on logging: enable per-token latency histograms in the console and export traces for any p99 spikes. That helps find whether spikes are due to scheduling, kernel stalls, or network.
[09:32] Jordan Lee: We're going to do a pilot with 2 H100 nodes, is that reasonable?
[09:36] Priya Singh: For initial pilot sure — we'll help you size based on your traffic mix. Two H100s can give you decent concurrency, but for isolation you may want to reserve capacity or use burst pools.
[09:45] Maya Patel: For the pilot, can Redwood run the benchmark from within our VPC or do we need to run externally?
[09:50] Alex Murray: We can run it in your VPC if you provide an agent; otherwise run the bench client and stream logs to us. For on-prem we'll provide the agent for the runtime.
[09:58] Jordan Lee: About deterministic results: random seeds and model temperature can change token lengths and latency. Any tips?
[10:03] Priya Singh: Freeze temperature/seed and use a representative prompt set. For function-calling traces, capture mean and tail lengths. Also run each config for long enough to capture warmup and steady-state (prefer 10-30 minutes per run).
[10:20] Samir Khan: You mentioned partial KV shard to disk earlier. How much overhead is disk-backed KV?
[10:24] Priya Singh: Disk-backed kv is much slower — it's a fallback to avoid OOMs. Expect high p99s if you hit disk; it's better than OOM but only for occasional long contexts. For steady high long-context workloads use more memory or shard across GPUs.
[10:38] Alex Murray: We're approaching the middle of the call but want to make sure we capture next steps.
[10:43] Jordan Lee: Two quick asks: (1) can you share the exact config we just discussed as a YAML? (2) can you include sample benchmark results for a similar customer?
[10:50] Priya Singh: Yes to both. We'll include YAML examples and a short benchmark summary (anonymized).
[10:56] Maya Patel: One more question — does Redwood support dynamic reconfiguration of max_num_seqs without restarting the pool?
[11:02] Priya Singh: Yes many knobs are dynamic via the console or API; some deep kernel-level changes require a restart. max_num_seqs and max_batch_latency are dynamic.
[11:12] Samir Khan: Great. Anything else on quantization: should we do offline conversion or on-the-fly conversion?
[11:18] Priya Singh: Offline conversion (GPTQ pipeline) yields better quality; on-the-fly quant can be used for fast experiments but is less optimal. For production use offline quant and validate with evals.
[11:29] Alex Murray: We're going to package the playbook, sample YAMLs, and the bench client. We'll also include a short checklist for VPC/on-prem setup (KMS, agent, audit logs).
[11:42] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. We'll try the bench this week and aim to share results by the 20th.
[11:48] Maya Patel: We may have a follow-up question about token accounting — can we loop in your solutions engineer?
[11:52] Alex Murray: Priya will lead that.
[11:55] Priya Singh: Yup, I'll be available to review logs and help tune the knobs.
[11:58] Samir Khan: Thanks all.
